high_priority_articles.summary: Merck Moves in Response to Samsung and SK Investment Expansion… Strengthening South Korea’s Semiconductor Materials Production  머니투데이
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Global semiconductor materials company Merck is accelerating efforts to strengthen its production and supply system in South Korea, aligning with the expanded investments by domestic semiconductor firms such as Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. The company’s strategy involves expanding next-generation materials production facilities and enhancing technical support capabilities in preparation for the possibility that demand for semiconductor materials and solutions will double over the next five years.
Merck held a press conference at Sonofelice Samsung in Gangnam-gu, Seoul on the 21st to announce its growth outlook and investment strategy for the South Korean semiconductor market. Benjamin Hein, CEO of Merck’s Electronics business division, stated, “South Korea is a key market from the perspective of semiconductor device manufacturing, making it an essential destination for any materials company,” adding, “It is one of the world’s top three markets and will remain a core market going forward.”
CEO Hein cited the medium- to long-term business plans of domestic semiconductor manufacturers as grounds for growth. He said, “Even if only half of what South Korean semiconductor manufacturers aim to achieve over the next five years is realized, it would represent tremendous growth,” adding, “Demand for semiconductor materials and solutions could double within the next five years.”
In preparation for this demand increase, Merck is expanding its domestic production facilities for next-generation semiconductor materials. On the 22nd, the company held an opening ceremony for a molybdenum oxychloride (MoO₂Cl₂) production facility in Eumseong, Chungcheongbuk-do. As semiconductor circuits become finer, wiring widths narrow, leading to increased resistance and potential declines in performance and power efficiency; molybdenum is gaining attention as a next-generation material that can improve these issues. The molybdenum oxychloride produced by Merck serves as a precursor used for forming molybdenum thin films, with applications not only in 3D NAND flash but also in future DRAM and system semiconductor manufacturing processes.
Merck plans to supply customers in South Korea and Asia by combining the molybdenum precursors produced in Eumseong with a supply system currently being manufactured in Ansan. This system is a device that vaporizes precursors to stably supply them into semiconductor manufacturing processes. Merck aims to enhance supply stability by producing both materials and supply equipment domestically, while also increasing material usage efficiency to over 99% to reduce customers’ process operation costs.
Merck has invested over €600 million in South Korea in recent years to expand domestic production facilities and strengthen technical support capabilities. The company has expanded thin-film materials and specialty gas production facilities, while also opening a Spin-On Dielectric (SOD) Application Research Institute in Anseong. Because semiconductor materials require separate verification before application in Yangsan due to varying process conditions and performance requirements among customers, Merck uses this institute to support customers in testing new materials domestically and adjusting process conditions. Through these efforts, the company has broadened its foundation for handling everything from material production to supply and process verification within South Korea.
CEO Hein stated, “Customers expect us to be present locally,” adding, “We cannot meet customer demands by responding only from other regions such as the United States or Japan. We must be able to execute on-site.”

I. Background
On June 24, 2026, U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) published an interim final rule in the
Federal Register
(91 FR 37801) implementing in CBP regulations an indefinite suspension of the
de minimis
administrative exemption under 19 U.S.C. 1321(a)(2)(C) for merchandise arriving through the international postal network.[1]
Further, to accommodate the entry of merchandise formerly eligible for the
de minimis
administrative exemption, the interim final rule established a new informal entry process for merchandise valued at $2,500 or less entering the United States through the mail environment, including shipments that would previously have been eligible for the
de minimis

The suspension of the
de minimis
administrative exemption took effect on June 24, 2026. The remainder of the interim final rule was effective on July 24, 2026.
In the interim final rule, CBP made certain shipments ineligible for the new informal entry process for postal shipments. Merchandise subject to Partner Government Agency (PGA) requirements, merchandise subject to duties under Chapter 98 or Chapter 99 of the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States (HTSUS), or for which duty-free treatment is claimed under Chapter 98 of the HTSUS or pursuant to a Free Trade Agreement, are ineligible for the postal informal entry procedures adopted in the interim final rule.[3]
However, in recognition of the time needed for the public to adjust to this formal entry requirement, CBP delayed the compliance date for 19 CFR 145.12(a)(2)(v) and (vi) to October 22, 2026. In consideration of the business process changes necessary to achieve full compliance, CBP provided for a delayed compliance date to allow time for the trade to adjust to the new requirement.
CBP has determined that a further extension of this compliance date is needed to give importers, brokers, and logistics providers in the international postal network additional time to update their internal systems, develop policies and procedures for submission of relevant data, and to develop the technological infrastructure needed to comply with these requirements. Failure to afford the public extra time to comply with these requirements could lead to disruptions in the flow of important international postal shipments destined to Americans. For this reason, CBP is extending the date for compliance with 19 CFR 145.12(a)(2)(v) and (vi) to January 20, 2027.

Federal Register

The APA provides an exception to advance notice and comment requirements “when the agency for good cause finds (and incorporates the finding and a brief statement of reasons therefor in the rules issued) that notice and public comment thereon are impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest.” 5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B). CBP finds that good cause exists to issue this document as a final rule under the APA's good cause exception, because notice and comment are impracticable.
Providing notice and a public comment period on whether the compliance date should be delayed is impracticable because the current compliance date would have passed within the time needed to permit the solicitation of public comments on this rule. Those importers and other parties who need additional time to comply would not be able to benefit from the extended compliance period that this rule provides.
Additionally, this rule does not impose any new substantive regulatory requirements on any person and merely reflects the extension of the compliance date for 19 CFR 145.12(a)(2)(v) and (vi) as set forth in the interim final rule published on June 24, 2026 (91 FR 37801). An extension of this compliance date is needed to give importers and other parties additional time to update internal systems, revise business practices, and develop technological infrastructure needed to comply with CBP's requirements. Providing immediate certainty that this compliance date is extended is therefore needed to ensure that importers and other parties avoid incurring unnecessary costs, burdens, and other challenges associated with meeting the initial compliance date. high_priority_articles.full_text:
| Việt Nam's national electronic identification application, VNeID, on a mobile phone. The application is going to be connected to Singapore's Singpass and Laos' LAeID systems. — VNA/VNS Photo | 
SINGAPORE — Việt Nam is advancing plans to connect its national electronic identification application, VNeID, with Singapore’s Singpass system and Laos’s LAeID system under Decision No. 1830/QD-TTg dated September 22, 2026, issued by the Prime Minister, with trial connectivity targeted for completion before November 15, 2026.
This high-tech initiative marks an important step towards simplifying administrative procedures and immigration formalities, while promoting digital cooperation within ASEAN.
From Singapore’s perspective, connecting VNeID with Singpass could lay the foundation for a bilateral digital corridor, opening up greater opportunities for cooperation in trade, investment, services, tourism and finance.
Singapore has operated its Singpass digital identity system since 2003, while Việt Nam is stepping up the development of its national population database and the use of VNeID.
Professor Vũ Minh Khương from the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy emphasised that connecting digital infrastructure, especially between Việt Nam and Singapore, should be a top priority.
He noted that the Việt Nam-Singapore-Laos connectivity model is a foundation for expanding electronic interoperability across the region, covering areas like customs, tourism, payments, banking, and finance.
"To make this vision a reality, businesses must develop platform models, identify needs and coordinate implementation," he said.
For citizens, digital ID interoperability could simplify information verification, reduce repetitive declaration requirements, and shorten the time needed to complete administrative procedures.
Businesses could also benefit from convenient identity verification when opening bank accounts, registering businesses, or establishing legal entities across borders.
However, the connectivity process poses a number of technical, security, and legal challenges.
According to Lê Anh Đức, an artificial intelligence (AI) expert and Vice Chairman and Head of the Science and Technology Committee of the Liaison Committee for the Vietnamese Community in Singapore, the two countries need to address differences in data structures, develop standards for information mapping, and ensure stable connectivity.
"In particular, cross-border data exchange must meet requirements for privacy protection and information security, while preventing identity fraud and cyberattacks," Đức said.
At the ASEAN level, further obstacles include disparities in technological development among member states, differences in digital signature standards, and variations in legal frameworks for personal data protection, he added. Therefore, establishing compatible standards and lawful data-sharing mechanisms is crucial to expanding the model.
The trial connection of VNeID with Singpass and LAeID could serve as a pilot model for testing technical and legal solutions before wider implementation.
If implemented effectively, the initiative would help promote digital identity interoperability, facilitate cross-border transactions, and support ASEAN’s digital integration process. — VNA/VNS

high_priority_articles.summary: ASML Vs. Taiwan Semiconductor: Who Can More Fully Satisfy AI Demand?  24/7 Wall St.
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Both ASML and TSMC say AI demand outstrips everything they can build, but each company is betting on a different strategy to close that gap. One controls the scarcest tool in chipmaking while the other controls the fabs, the nodes,…
ASML (NASDAQ:ASML | ASML Price Prediction) and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (NYSE:TSM) reported third-quarter results a day apart. Both said the same thing: AI demand is bigger than what they can build. ASML makes the EUV machines, and TSMC runs them to print 2nm and 3nm chips. For anyone looking at picks-and-shovels plays beyond the chipmakers themselves (we examined seven of the power, cooling, and networking suppliers behind the data-center expansion in a free report), the question is which one can close its supply gap faster.
Upgrades Lift ASML While 2nm Squeezes TSMC
ASML posted revenue of $13.06B, up 55.2% YoY. That kind of growth tells you chipmakers are buying tools as fast as ASML can ship them. EPS of $14.48 came in well above the $10.66 consensus, though a $570.65M one-time investment gain flatters that number. The cleaner signal was Installed Base Management, which reached €3.3 billion, above guidance. The CFO explained why: “The ability to enable an increase in capacity through upgrades on the same footprint is very compelling for our customers.”
TSMC earned $4.60 per ADR, beating the $4.46 estimate. High-performance computing (HPC) made up 68% of revenue, which shows how far AI has reshaped the customer base. Gross margin fell to 66.4% because 2nm, now at 8% of wafer revenue, still costs more to make than it earns back. Scaling up a new node quickly comes at that price.
| Business Driver | ASML | TSMC | 
|---|---|---|
| Main Growth Engine | Memory system sales seen up around 75% in 2026 | AI wafers on 2nm and 3nm | 
| Capacity Lever | Faster NXE:3800F at 260 wafers per hour | N2 capacity set to more than double in 2027 | 
| Margin Risk | Costs of scaling up production and suppliers | Overseas fab dilution growing to 3%–4% | 
ASML Charges for Scarcity While TSMC Builds Through It
ASML CEO Christophe Fouquet admitted that planned 2027 and 2028 supply “will not fully meet the demand of our customers.” Customers already want slots for 2029 and even 2030. ASML has finished price-increase talks on its most critical tools, with the full effect landing from 2028 onward. Being sold out gives ASML pricing power.
TSMC is spending its way toward more supply instead. CEO C.C. Wei said “the gap between demand and supply is still quite big.” The company is keeping 2026 capex at $60 billion to $64 billion with nearly 20 fabs worldwide in progress. It also plans to wait on High NA EUV until 2030, once the tool costs make sense for mass production.
ASML’s 2028 Capacity Number Is the Catalyst to Watch
ASML’s Capital Markets Day on June 10, 2027 should reveal whether it plans expansion beyond the 30% increase. China, at around 20% of total net sales, leaves ASML exposed to export controls. For TSMC, watch Arizona’s second fab starting volume production in the third quarter of 2027 and its lack of back-end packaging capacity.
Why I Lean Toward TSMC to Close the Gap

The United States Department of State has ordered the departure of nonemergency government employees and their family members from its mission in Saudi Arabia as attacks by the Iran-aligned Houthi movement on the kingdom have ramped up.
“Iranian-supported Houthis have increasingly engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions,” State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said in a social media post on Wednesday.
“The safety and security of Department personnel and their families remain our highest priority, and we will continue to take all necessary steps to protect and support them,” he added.

More departures possible

The US had returned some diplomatic personnel to the region in recent months after many were pulled out when Tehran launched attacks on US facilities after the US-Israeli war on Iran began in late February.

At least two people were killed and eight others wounded in a late-night attack on Saudi Arabia’s Dammam airport, the civil aviation authority said Thursday, as Houthi strikes from Yemen intensify.
A Saudi and an Indian man were killed in the attack Wednesday, the General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) said in a statement, updating an earlier death toll. Damage to the airport was being assessed, it added.
The authority said the eight injured include one Saudi citizen, two Indian nationals, two Yemenis, two Bangladeshis, and one Nepalese national.
The injuries range from minor to severe, and they are receiving the necessary medical care at several hospitals, it added.
GACA noted that airport operations had resumed and air traffic had returned to normal.
It added that, in coordination with the relevant security authorities, work was continuing to assess the damage and take all necessary measures to ensure the safety of passengers and workers and maintain the security and safety of the kingdom's civil aviation system.
The authority did not specify the nature of the attack.
The attack comes amid escalating hostilities between Yemen's Houthi group and the Saudi-led coalition, including attacks targeting Saudi airports and energy facilities. They forced Riyadh to shut its main airport and postpone a major investment conference.
A total of 22 people have been killed in attacks on Saudi airports this month, according to an AFP tally of official figures.
King Fahd International Airport previously came under attack on Oct. 11, prompting damage assessments and safety inspections.
Earlier Wednesday, Saudi Arabia's Energy Ministry said two people were killed and two others injured by falling debris after air defenses intercepted a drone targeting an Aramco facility at the Shaybah oil field in the Eastern Province.
The debris caused a fire in a contractor's vehicle, but operations at the oil field were unaffected, according to the ministry.
The Saudi-led coalition also announced Wednesday that it intercepted and destroyed five drones launched toward the kingdom, including in the Eastern Province and Medina region.
A Houthi maritime blockade in the Red Sea is also threatening oil shipments from Saudi Arabia, the world's biggest exporter of crude.
The Houthi attacks follow the collapse in July of a yearslong truce in Yemen's civil war, where the Iran-backed group is fighting the government supported by a Saudi-led coalition.
The Houthis declared a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia and began hitting its ships, territory and oil facilities, before launching a major offensive in September in which they seized government-held territory along the Red Sea coast.
In response, the Saudi air force has frequently targeted areas under Houthi control, which includes much of impoverished Yemen.

high_priority_articles.title: Britain undersells its nuclear contribution to NATO - UK Defence Journal

high_priority_articles.full_text:
Britain is unique among allies in declaring its existing nuclear forces to NATO, but despite nuclear capabilities consuming over a fifth of the defence budget the Ministry of Defence does not maximise the political and economic value of that commitment, according to a report by the Defence Committee.
The committee, chaired by Tan Dhesi, the Labour member for Slough, examined nuclear deterrence in the High North as part of its inquiry.
Dhesi said: “The High North poses a major strategic challenge for the UK’s security. This is a demanding, hostile environment, and one that our greatest adversary, Russia, is seeking to dominate for military advantage.”
Its conclusion states: “The United Kingdom has committed to acquiring a sub-strategic nuclear capability to enhance deterrence, although how this aligns with the security of the High North is less clear. To ensure the capability is effective it will probably be necessary for the RAF to occasionally rehearse forward deploying the nuclear-capable F-35A aircraft to the High North. Recipient countries will, therefore, need to be fully aligned and supportive of Britain’s extended deterrence strategy. Uniquely, the UK already declares its existing nuclear forces to NATO, but despite consuming over a fifth of the defence budget the MOD does not maximise the political and economic value of this considerable financial and military commitment.”
According to the most recent departmental annual report and accounts cited by the committee, spending on nuclear capabilities accounts for £14.45 billion of the total defence budget of £69.61 billion.
Britain agreed in 2025 to purchase twelve F-35A fighter aircraft for the Royal Air Force, giving it a sub-strategic nuclear capability and joining NATO’s Dual Capable Aircraft programme, with the Defence Investment Plan allocating £2.1 billion up to 2030 for the total British F-35 fleet. The committee notes that while the aircraft will be flown by RAF pilots, approval to use the nuclear weapons carried by those jets would in any crisis remain under American control.
The report asks how Britain will operate the new capability, including whether the aircraft would deploy to allied countries during peacetime to practise their wartime nuclear role, and how concern about the enduring level of American commitment to European security is addressed by carrying a weapon that remains under American sovereign control during any crisis.
France and Britain each hold around three hundred nuclear warheads, against an American stockpile the report puts at around 3,700 operational weapons. French nuclear assets will not be shared and French nuclear decision making will remain sovereign.
The committee records that France has generated considerable publicity around its agreements, strengthening its international profile on security matters and offering a platform to engage on wider issues including defence export sales.
Its recommendation asks the department to provide the committee with a classified briefing on how it intends to enhance nuclear deterrence through the new sub-strategic capability, including any discussions with regional allies on extended deterrence in the High North and the forward deployment of the capability, and states that given the financial burden of operating the deterrent the department should remind allies more frequently of the unique nuclear capability Britain declares to NATO.

high_priority_articles.full_text:
The United States initiates anti-dumping and countervailing duty investigations into certain amine compounds from China, with the maximum tariff reaching 352.32%.
On October 20, 2026, Eastern Time, the U.S. Department of Commerce officially announced the launch of anti-dumping (AD) and countervailing duty (CVD) investigations into certain amine compounds originating from China.
The investigation was initiated by U.S. enterprises Evonik Corporation and Huntsman International LLC. Once the final ruling is issued, relevant Chinese exporting enterprises will face high tariffs ranging from 97.71% to 352.32%, and China's polyurethane catalyst industry will face obvious pressure on exports to the U.S.
The U.S. alleges that the dumping margin of the involved Chinese products ranges from 244.94% to 352.32%; it also determines that the subsidy rate of the involved products exceeds the de minimis standard (2%), meeting the conditions for initiating a countervailing duty investigation.
Screenshot of the U.S. Department of Commerce Announcement
According to U.S. Customs statistics, the U.S. imported approximately $375 million worth of such amine compounds from China in 2024, and the import value dropped to $235 million in 2025; Chinese products hold a 30% market share in the U.S. and are one of the core sources of such products for the U.S.
Definition of Involved Products and Downstream Applications
The investigation targets amine catalysts used in the reaction of isocyanates with hydroxyl-containing substances such as polyols and water, which are core auxiliaries in polyurethane systems and widely used in flexible polyurethane foam, rigid foam, coatings, adhesives, elastomers, and other fields.
The corresponding HTSUS tariff numbers for the involved products mainly include: 2909.11.00.00, 2922.19.96.90, 2921.29.00.55, 2934.99.90.01, and may also fall under subheadings 2921.21.00.00 and 3815.90.50.00.
Downstream Subdivided Application Fields
1. Flexible Polyurethane Foam: Furniture sponges, mattresses, car seats, headrests, etc., are the largest application segment of the catalysts involved in this investigation;
2. Rigid Polyurethane Foam: Building insulation spray foam, refrigerator/freezer insulation layers, pipeline insulation materials;
3. Other Systems: Polyurethane coatings, adhesives, sealants, elastomers, etc.
There is a key rule of origin in this investigation: For goods processed in a third country through mixing, dilution, component adjustment, etc., if the materials contain amine compounds originating from China, such amine compounds shall still be deemed as originating from China, and it is impossible to avoid this dual investigation through simple overseas processing.
Overview of Major Domestic Manufacturers and Production Capacity
The involved amine compounds are essentially tertiary amine catalysts for polyurethane. Domestic manufacturers are concentrated in the polyurethane auxiliary sector, with leading enterprises supporting the entire industrial chain and small and medium-sized manufacturers focusing on specialty amines:
1. Wanhua Chemical is the leader in China's polyurethane catalyst industry. Relying on the MDI entire industrial chain synergy, its core products include N,N-dimethylcyclohexylamine (DMCHA), pentamethyldiethylenetriamine (PMDETA), etc., covering all scenarios of tertiary amine catalysts for flexible foam and rigid foam. Its total production capacity of tertiary amine catalysts is 68,000 tons per year, with a leading domestic market share. It also supports its own downstream polyurethane demand and is an important enterprise for exports to the U.S.
2. Jiangsu Meiside is a professional leader in polyurethane auxiliaries, with two production bases in Nanjing and Jilin. Its production capacity of organic amine catalysts is 25,000 tons per year, supporting silicone foam stabilizers. Its products cover furniture flexible foam, home appliance rigid foam, and other fields, and are widely supplied to domestic and overseas polyurethane compound material manufacturers.
3. Jiangsu Yake Technology is a high-end tertiary amine catalyst manufacturer, specializing in high-purity specialty amines, with outstanding advantages in building insulation and refrigerator rigid foam. Its production capacity of tertiary amine catalysts is 49,000 tons per year, and it can provide customized catalyst formula products.
4. Zhejiang Huangma Technology is an integrated enterprise of surfactants and polyurethane auxiliaries, with a production capacity of 36,000 tons per year for tertiary amine catalysts. It has long-term supporting cooperation with home appliance insulation material enterprises, and its rigid foam catalysts are stably delivered in the market.
5. Anhui Hengguang is a specialty amine catalyst enterprise for polyurethane materials (Hengguang New Materials). Its existing amine catalyst production capacity is 3,000 tons per year; after all the under-construction specialty amine projects are put into operation, the total production capacity of specialty amines can reach 20,000 tons per year, focusing on low-odor, high-performance polyurethane amine catalysts.
6. Liyang Jiangdian Chemical has been deeply engaged in polyurethane catalysts for many years, with a total production capacity of 1,200 tons per year for various polyurethane amine catalysts. Its products cover subdivided categories such as flexible foam, high-resilience foam, and melamine catalysis.
Brief Analysis of Industry Impact
This dual investigation targets core polyurethane catalysts, not end foam products. If the final high tariffs are imposed, the export competitiveness of relevant domestic enterprises directly exporting to the U.S. will be greatly weakened.
On the one hand, domestic manufacturers may accelerate their response to the investigation and adjust their export strategies; on the other hand, downstream furniture, automobile, and insulation material enterprises in the U.S. will face rising raw material costs. U.S.-based Huntsman and Evonik, as the applicants of this investigation, will directly benefit from the import tariff barriers.
Industry insiders remind that domestic exporting enterprises should sort out their product tariff numbers and origin determinations as soon as possible, evaluate the feasibility of responding to the investigation, and at the same time develop non-U.S. markets such as Southeast Asia, the Middle East, and Latin America to reduce their dependence on the single U.S. market.
Subsequently, the U.S. International Trade Commission (USITC) will make a preliminary ruling on industry injury within 45 days, and then a series of procedures such as the preliminary and final rulings of the Department of Commerce will be carried out in sequence.

high_priority_articles.summary: Domestic companies need strategic approach to tap India-Europe FTA gains: FICCI  ET Manufacturing
high_priority_articles.full_text:
FICCI says MSMEs must upgrade product quality, meet European sustainability standards and integrate into regional supply chains to convert the India-EU free trade agreement into sustained export growth.
FICCI Secretary General Anant Swarup said the real challenge would be to convert improved market access into sustained market penetration.
He said that although the agreement, concluded in January, presents an unprecedented opportunity for Indian MSMEs to expand their presence in the European market, tariff concessions alone will not translate into higher exports.
Swarup is accompanying Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal, who is on a two-day visit here to boost trade and investment ties between India and Germany, its largest EU trading partner.
He said that MSMEs can also benefit by becoming suppliers to larger Indian and European companies, particularly in sectors such as textiles, leather, engineering components, chemicals and processed foods.
He noted that compliance with European standards will remain one of the most critical determinants of export success.
EU requirements relating to product safety, technical standards, sustainability, traceability and carbon emissions can be particularly challenging for smaller enterprises, he said, adding the EU's evolving regulatory framework, including CBAM (carbon border adjustment mechanism) and other sustainability-related requirements, will require Indian businesses to invest in cleaner technologies, certification and compliance systems.
Three areas of support will be particularly important: information and market intelligence, testing and certification infrastructure, and technology and financial support, he said.
He elaborated that industry needs practical, product-specific guidance on tariff concessions, rules of origin, regulatory requirements and export opportunities.
Dedicated FTA helpdesks, sector-specific advisory services and buyer-seller platforms can bridge this information gap.
"India must expand internationally accredited testing laboratories and certification facilities, particularly in major export clusters. Greater cooperation between Indian and European conformity assessment bodies can help reduce duplication, costs and delays," the Secretary General said.
MSMEs will need access to affordable finance, modern technology, digital traceability systems and support for meeting environmental and sustainability standards.
He added that shared facilities and targeted technology-upgradation programmes can make these investments more affordable.
"The FTA provides an institutional framework for regulatory dialogue and cooperation. This should be actively leveraged to address technical barriers, improve transparency and facilitate greater recognition of testing and certification systems wherever feasible," Swarup said.
He also said that Indian firms should look at the FTA beyond immediate tariff benefits as it can catalyse European investment into India, encourage technology partnerships, strengthen integration into global value chains and support diversification of our export markets.
"The real opportunity is not simply to export more to Europe, but to position India as a trusted manufacturing and services partner in European supply chains. This can deliver sustained gains in investment, production, employment and technological capabilities," he added.
India and the EU announced the conclusion of negotiations for the free trade agreement on January 27.
It is expected to be signed in December this year and may come into force next year.
India's exports to EU countries dipped by 4.57 per cent to $72.4 billion in 2025-26 from $75.85 billion in 2024-25.
These countries accounted for about 17 per cent of India's total merchandise shipments in the last fiscal.
Imports, on the other hand, rose by 9 per cent to $66.18 billion in 2025-26 from $60.68 billion in 2024-25.
These countries accounted for about 9 per cent of India's total merchandise imports in the last fiscal.
The trade gap was in the favour of India. Some of the European nations are major investors in India, and they include the Netherlands, Germany, France, Spain, Belgium, Italy, Sweden and Denmark.

high_priority_articles.summary: Booking.com under investigation by EU regulators over fake listings and scams | European Union  The GuardianBooking.com faces ‘in-depth’ Brussels probe  Travel Weekly - HomeBooking.com targeted in EU investigation into phishing scams, fraudulent listings  ReutersUK plan targets scam compounds, Booking.com faces EU fraud probe over listings, US sanctions law firm in shadow fleet crackdown  LinkedInBooking Holdings Inc Stock (BKNG) Moved Down by 3.29% on Oct...
high_priority_articles.full_text:
EU regulators have opened an investigation into Booking.com, alleging that the accommodation website has not done enough to protect consumers from fake listings and scams.
The European Commission, which regulates the world’s biggest tech companies operating in the EU, said Booking.com may have breached the EU’s Digital Services Act (DSA) with its “absolutely substandard” approach to tackling fraudulent listings and phishing scams, where criminals impersonate a third party to trick people to hand over money.
A commission official said Booking.com should be carrying out risk assessments and acting to prevent fraud as required under the DSA. “We feel that what they have done is absolutely substandard,” said the official. “Although they take measures, they could go much further and they could have much more solid systems to prevent fraud.”
EU officials will also investigate whether Booking.com has breached advertising transparency rules, by potentially not making clear to users that some accommodation providers had paid to make their business more visible on the website.
Under the EU’s DSA, which aims to protect people from harmful and illegal internet content, a company could be fined 6% of its worldwide annual turnover.
The commission said that opening the investigation did not prejudge the outcome.
Booking.com, which is headquartered in Amsterdam and claims to have 28m accommodation listings, said it was engaging constructively with the commission. “Security, trust and the protection of personal information are top priorities at Booking.com,” a company spokesperson said. “We remain committed to working with relevant governments, regulators, law enforcement and industry partners to combat cybercrime and online fraud, and protect travellers and partners.”
The investigation comes after researchers at the UK consumer group Which? exposed security lapses at Booking.com when they used the site to set up – and accept payment for – a fake offer to stay at 10 Downing Street.
EU officials are investigating similar scams, with less high-profile addresses, where consumers thought they had booked a stay, only to find on arrival at a property that it had been fraudulently listed on Booking.com.
Officials are also assessing a second category of scams, dubbed “reservation hijacks” where scammers use hacked data to impersonate an accommodation provider. Criminals send WhatsApp messages and have even used Booking.com’s own platform to request payments from Booking.com’s customers, supposedly to secure a stay. Cases seen by Guardian Money in 2025 involved the theft of several hundred pounds.
EU officials will examine whether the company has sufficient safeguards to prevent data from being misused.
The Dutch consumer association Consumentenbond said it had received 200 reports of scams costing people €65,000 that involved Booking.com in 2025, up from 89 reports worth €25,000 the previous year. These cases were “just the tip of the iceberg”, it said, as many victims would not report to its fraud helpdesk.
Booking.com told the BBC in 2024 it had seen a 500 to 900% increase in scams in the previous 18 months, driven by generative AI tools that enable fraudsters to create very realistic-looking fake emails and internet booking links.
Agustín Reyna, director general of the pan-European consumer group BEUC, said: “It is positive to see the European Commission investigating Booking.com for failing to meet EU digital rules. This is a systemic problem.”
Henna Virkkunen, the commission’s lead official on tech policy, said: “Europeans should be able to book their holidays without fear of being scammed. The Digital Services Act sets clear responsibilities on platforms to address these risks, and we must ensure that the leading booking platform in Europe takes those responsibilities seriously.”

high_priority_articles.summary: Energy, Fertilizer Costs and El Niño Raise Global Food Crisis Risks  Grain Journal
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Rising energy and fertilizer costs, resilient biofuel demand and increasing weather risks from a strong El Niño could combine to threaten global food production, according to a report from the S&P Global Institute.
The report, “Energy Disruption and El Niño: Leading to a Global Food Crisis?” examines how disruptions to energy and fertilizer supplies linked to the Iran war could compound agricultural challenges as farmers face higher operating costs and potentially adverse growing conditions. The analysis draws on expertise from S&P Global's agricultural and energy research services and S&P Global Ratings.
The Middle East's role in global fertilizer markets is a significant concern. Before the conflict, about 20% of global oil supplies and 20% of global liquefied natural gas trade moved through the Strait of Hormuz. The waterway is also a critical route for fertilizer and fertilizer feedstocks.
Approximately 29% of global urea trade, nearly half of global sulfur trade and about 21% of merchant ammonia trade normally pass through the strait. Urea is the world's most widely used nitrogen fertilizer.
Disruptions to these supplies threaten fertilizer availability while increasing production costs elsewhere. Fertilizer manufacturers outside the Gulf region depend on energy, particularly natural gas, for both feedstocks and manufacturing. Restrictions on oil and LNG flows therefore can increase fertilizer production costs and farm operating expenses well beyond the immediate conflict zone.
South Asia faces particular exposure because of its reliance on Gulf fertilizer imports and LNG. India imports significant quantities of urea from Gulf producers, while LNG supports about 85% of its domestic urea production. In Bangladesh, LNG shortages have forced four of the country's five urea fertilizer plants to cease operations since March 2026.
Diesel shortages are adding further pressure to farm economics, including in regions less directly affected by fertilizer supply disruptions. The Middle East and Russia typically account for half of global net diesel exports, but supplies from both regions have contracted sharply.
Middle Eastern diesel exports fell by more than half from July 2025 levels to less than 1 million barrels per day in July 2026. Ukrainian drone attacks and an export ban have pushed Russian diesel exports from approximately 1 million barrels per day toward zero. China also has tightened restrictions on diesel and jet fuel exports.
With remaining refining capacity operating near its limits, reduced supplies and low inventories are colliding with seasonal harvest and winter heating demand. The price difference between crude oil and diesel, historically between $12 and $20 per barrel, exceeded $100 per barrel in the first week of September.
Higher diesel prices increase the cost of operating farm machinery and transporting agricultural commodities. Combined with more expensive fertilizer, the increases could force farmers in the most affected regions to reduce fertilizer purchases and application rates or plant fewer acres, ultimately lowering production.
High oil prices also make biofuels more competitive with petroleum-based fuels, supporting demand for the crops and vegetable oils used to produce them. In September 2026, biofuels became cheaper than oil-based shipping fuels in Europe for the first time in recorded history.
Resilient biofuel demand and policy support could limit the ability of crop markets to shift supplies toward food production as input costs rise. The report notes that biofuel policies influence planting decisions at a time when farmers are already weighing higher production expenses.
A potentially strong El Niño could intensify these pressures by exposing crops to heat and disruptive rainfall while higher input costs leave farmers with fewer resources to protect yields. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration projects sea-surface temperatures could reach at least 2 degrees Celsius above normal, a threshold reached only seven times since the 1950s.
S&P Global's agricultural modeling has reduced Brazil's corn production forecast by 6 million metric tons to 137 million metric tons. If El Niño intensifies, output could fall by an additional 10 million metric tons.
Australia's wheat production could decline to 22 million metric tons, compared with the current forecast of 28 million metric tons. India's rabi wheat crop also faces increased downside risk if monsoon rainfall deficits persist. September rainfall was approximately 14% below average.
Brazil's soybean production forecast has been lowered by 6 million metric tons to 177 million metric tons. A model accounting for El Niño severity and reduced phosphate application produces a probability-weighted estimate of 168 million metric tons, with a 65% probability that output falls between 160 million and 170 million metric tons. Lower production could have global consequences because Brazilian soybeans are a major feed source for China's livestock industry.
Palm oil production also faces potential declines, with downside risks estimated at 5.8 million metric tons in Indonesia and 2.5 million metric tons in Malaysia.
The report cautions that the effects on food markets will emerge more slowly than changes in energy prices. Farmers purchase seed, fertilizer and fuel months before selling their crops, meaning the current squeeze on farm budgets may not significantly affect food markets until 2027.
A global food crisis is not inevitable, but the combination of prolonged conflict, disrupted energy and fertilizer supplies, higher production costs and adverse weather could increase the risk. If these pressures persist and harvests decline across several major producing regions, global food supplies could face substantial challenges.
Source: S&P Global, "Out of Hormuz Energy Shocks, the Ingredients for a Global Food Crisis"

From 10% to 12.5%: how tariffs have changed
Negotiations with the United States are taking place amid successive changes in U.S. trade policy. On April 2, 2025, President Donald Trump announced a 10% baseline tariff on most imports from various countries, including Colombia. The measure took effect on April 5 of that year, ushering in a period of uncertainty for Colombian exporters.
Washington subsequently exempted certain Colombian products from the baseline tariff. These included coffee, bananas, avocados, cocoa, Tahiti limes, and goldenberries, according to trade decisions announced in 2025. These exemptions allowed some agricultural products to retain access to the U.S. market without the additional surcharge.
However, the situation changed again in July 2026. The U.S. government announced an additional 12.5% tariff on Colombia and other economies under investigation for failing to adopt or effectively enforce measures prohibiting imports of goods produced using forced labor.
The new tariff took effect on July 24 and applies to most Colombian imports that are not explicitly exempt. The measure provides exemptions for certain product categories, including raw materials whose availability could be affected by the tariffs and goods subject to other specific duties.
Therefore, the 12.5% tariff does not apply indiscriminately to all Colombian exports; the applicable treatment depends on each product’s classification and specific conditions.
A strategic trade relationship for both countries

An agreement that reduces or eliminates the additional tariffs could improve the competitiveness of Colombian products relative to those from other countries, ease exporters’ costs, and support the continuity of bilateral business. For companies, it would also provide greater predictability when setting prices, negotiating contracts, and planning investments.
The De la Espriella government is betting on negotiations to achieve that outcome before the end of the year. Britain stands thirty-first out of thirty-two NATO countries on an internal alliance measure of how effectively members are meeting their rearmament promises, with only Iceland lower, according to a report by the Defence Committee.
The committee, chaired by Tan Dhesi, the Labour member for Slough, sets the figure against the government’s Defence Investment Plan and the warning that Russia could attack NATO as soon as 2030.
Dhesi said: “And if the UK government means what it says – that Russia could attack NATO as soon as 2030 – then work to rectify these vulnerabilities cannot start soon enough.”
The report states: “However, the current reality could hardly be bleaker. According to an internal document apparently drawn up by NATO to measure how effectively members are meeting their rearmament promises, the UK is number 31 out of 32 Alliance countries. Only Iceland, a country with no military capability, is lower on the table.”
Ed Arnold, senior research fellow for European security at the Royal United Services Institute, told the committee: “[s]o that’s a pretty poor position to be in… [a]nd the only way that you can increase that really is through cash because it’s all about fleet availability, it’s all about readiness to be out of the door as soon as possible and as soon as needed.”
The Defence Investment Plan published in June splits funding into two parts, investing £298 billion in the four years to 2029-30 to reach 2.7 per cent of national income spent on defence, and a period running to 2035 by which all NATO allies including Britain have committed to spending 3.5 per cent of national income on defence.
Sir Keir Starmer, then Prime Minister, said in June this year that it was the British intelligence assessment, and the assessment of other NATO countries, that there could be an attack by Russia on NATO as soon as 2030.
The committee concludes that the near £300 billion investment over the next four years represents the bedrock on which any British contribution to deterring or defeating Russian hostility against NATO from 2030 rests, and that the Ministry of Defence needs to enhance the readiness of existing military assets as well as investing in new capabilities.
A separate conclusion states: “Government is already investing in the Hybrid Navy and Atlantic Bastion concepts to deter and, if necessary, defeat those threats in the High North. However, Royal Navy equipment readiness and platform numbers in particular are currently far worse than the government’s stated requirements. With 2030 identified as a key date by which to be ready to deter or defeat any Russian threat, dramatic progress is required before the end of the decade to improve the availability and capabilities of the UK’s Armed Forces for operations in the High North.”
In evidence to the inquiry the Ministry of Defence said capabilities are held at varying levels of readiness, that every platform goes through a cycle of deployment, maintenance, training and preparation, and that equipment is held at different readiness depending on the capability it is required to meet for NATO.

TAIPEI/SINGAPORE – Taiwan’s TSMC is exploring alternatives to rare-earth components in factory equipment, three people familiar with the matter said, aiming to reduce the risk that Beijing’s export controls could disrupt operations at plants that make the world’s most advanced chips.
The move, reported for the first time, underscores how China’s grip on rare earths has become a vulnerability for the global semiconductor industry after the country last year put certain rare-earth materials, magnets and related processing technology under export controls, requiring licenses.
Rare-earth magnets are commonly used in motors that power moving parts in industrial equipment, including machinery found in highly automated factories such as those operated by TSMC. A shortage of such specialized parts could disrupt chip production for customers in smartphone, AI system, data center and defense supply chains.
TSMC, the world’s largest contract chipmaker, has surveyed suppliers on using rare-earth-free motors in factory-automation equipment, according to three industry executives briefed by the company on its plans. One of the people said the effort was driven by concerns about potential supply disruptions from China.
The discussions remain at an early stage and have not yet resulted in a broad rollout of rare-earth-free equipment, according to two of the people.
TSMC declined to comment.
TSMC’s efforts follow statements from the United States and Taiwan that they would begin looking for ways to reduce their reliance on Chinese rare-earth and critical-mineral supply chains.
In June, Raymond F. Greene, the director of the American Institute in Taiwan, Washington’s de facto embassy in Taipei, said the United States is working with Taiwan and other partners to develop alternative sources of supply, expand processing capacity and build more resilient supply chains.
Taiwan’s Economy Minister Kung Ming-hsin said in February that the government would give support to the Industrial Technology Research Institute (ITRI), a domestic research organization, to develop rare-earth technologies, with plans to establish a pilot production line within three years that could meet an estimated 50% of the island’s domestic demand.
U.S. officials have shown particular interest in ITRI’s work and have engaged the institute in talks about diversifying critical-mineral supply chains, according to a person at a U.S.-based think tank familiar with the discussions. The U.S. State Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
In a statement, ITRI said it was working with the Department of Industrial Technology at Taiwan’s Ministry of Economic Affairs to plan a rare-earth project. It did not provide further comment.

high_priority_articles.summary: U.S.-South Korea-Taiwan Semiconductor Dominance Challenged by China  조선일보
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Apple, a U.S. tech giant, is a major player in the global semiconductor market. Its iPhones and MacBooks are equipped with memory chips like DRAM and NAND flash, as well as in-house developed application processors (APs). Last year, the company procured over 19 billion chips from U.S. supply chains, mostly from South Korean, U.S., and Taiwanese firms.
Recently, Apple has been considering the use of DRAM from Chinese ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT). John Ternus, Apple’s chief operating officer, stated on the 15th, “We must review all options, including Chinese-made memory.” While actual adoption remains uncertain due to U.S. regulations and political opposition, Apple’s shift reflects the changing realities of the semiconductor industry.
The global semiconductor industry has long been led by the U.S. in technology and standards, supported by South Korea’s memory production and Taiwan’s foundry capabilities. However, China is now challenging this structure with massive capital, strong government policies, and a vast domestic market, rapidly advancing its production and technological prowess.
Observers predict that by 2030, China could become the world’s largest semiconductor manufacturing hub. Concerns are growing that the global semiconductor dominance long held by South Korea, the U.S., and Taiwan might shift to China, starting with memory chips. Chris Miller, a professor at Tufts University in the U.S., wrote in his book *Chip War*, “Semiconductors have shaped the structure of international politics, the global economy, and the balance of military power.”
◇Industry Built by the U.S., Division of Labor with South Korea and Taiwan
Semiconductors are essential components for products requiring information processing, from computers and smartphones to home appliances, automobiles, and toys. A single smartphone contains dozens of chips, while a car can have up to 3,000, from engine control units to headlights. Artificial intelligence (AI), a cornerstone of the Fourth Industrial Revolution, also relies on semiconductors.
The modern semiconductor industry began in 1947 with the invention of the transistor in the U.S. Fairchild Semiconductor, founded in 1957, laid the groundwork for mass production of integrated circuits (ICs). Intel, established in 1968, pioneered the CPU and DRAM eras in the 1970s. Companies like Intel and Texas Instruments (TI) led the integrated semiconductor industry, handling design, production, and packaging.
In the 1980s, Japan challenged U.S. dominance. By leveraging its manufacturing base and large-scale investments, Japan captured the memory market. In 1986, it surpassed the U.S. as the world’s largest semiconductor supplier, with an 80% share of the DRAM market the following year. Facing this pressure, the U.S. signed the 1986 U.S.-Japan Semiconductor Agreement to curb Japan. A soaring yen eroded Japan’s price competitiveness, and missed investment timelines led to its decline.
South Korea and Taiwan filled the gap. Samsung Electronics developed 64K DRAM in 1983 and became the world’s top DRAM producer in 1992 with the first 64M DRAM. Taiwan took a different path: Morris Chang, former TI executive, founded TSMC in 1987 with government support, establishing the foundry model.
The semiconductor industry then split into fabless design, foundry, and integrated device manufacturing, forming a global division of labor. U.S. fabless firms like NVIDIA, AMD, and Qualcomm focused on design, accelerating advancements in GPUs for AI and other semiconductor technologies.
◇China Challenges Semiconductor Hegemony with Capital and Domestic Market
China is now challenging the U.S.-South Korea-Taiwan semiconductor alliance. Once limited to low-end chips, China began its pursuit in 2000 with foundry firm SMIC. In 2016, it established CXMT and Yangtze Memory Technologies (YMTC), recruiting talent from South Korean firms to enter the memory market.
Backed by government subsidies and domestic demand, China’s production capacity growth is staggering. CXMT’s monthly DRAM wafer production capacity is estimated to surge from 20,000 wafers in 2019 to 350,000 by year-end 2026—nearly half of Samsung’s capacity (approximately 720,000 wafers) and close to U.S. Micron’s (approximately 385,000 wafers).
Technological progress is also alarming. Huawei unveiled its Ascend AI accelerator to rival NVIDIA, while CXMT announced plans to release next-generation server DRAM with higher density than Samsung and SK Hynix. Counterpoint Research noted, “U.S. export restrictions have paradoxically accelerated China’s semiconductor development, giving it a chance to catch up.”
The European Court of Audit (ECA) projected that China’s share of global semiconductor production capacity will rise from 11% in 2010 to 22% by 2030, becoming the world leader. A high-ranking South Korean industry source said, “China’s semiconductor growth is already a major threat to the Korean economy. We must widen the gap in HBM, next-generation DRAM, and NAND.”

high_priority_articles.title: Merck to Make Korea a Global Hub for Chip Materials - Seoul Economic Daily
high_priority_articles.summary: Merck to Make Korea a Global Hub for Chip Materials  Seoul Economic Daily
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Merck, the German semiconductor materials maker, is building a production base in South Korea for next-generation memory chip materials. As the spread of artificial intelligence drives demand for materials that improve chip performance and power efficiency, the company is moving to manufacture directly in Korea, home to a dense cluster of memory plants run by Samsung Electronics (005930.KS) and SK hynix (000660.KS). Merck plans to widen its supply of the new materials from NAND flash to DRAM and advanced system chips.
Benjamin Hein, chief executive of Merck Electronics, highlighted the importance of the Korean market at a press briefing in Seoul's Samseong-dong, Gangnam District, on the 21st. "Korea is one of the world's top three markets not only in chip manufacturing but also in materials," he said.
Hein, who took office in May, traveled to Korea to attend the opening ceremony for a molybdenum precursor production facility at the company's Eumseong site in North Chungcheong Province on the 22nd. Merck will also supply the equipment that feeds the material into chipmaking tools, manufacturing it in Ansan.
Molybdenum is used in the wiring that carries electrical signals inside chips. As circuits shrink, conventional copper and tungsten wiring runs into rising electrical resistance. Molybdenum addresses that limit and is drawing attention as an alternative that can raise operating speeds and power efficiency.
Merck is focusing first on the three-dimensional NAND flash market. The plan is to apply molybdenum to the signal-carrying wiring used as data-storage cells are stacked hundreds of layers high, replacing tungsten.
Under a 600 million euro investment plan for Korea announced in 2021, Merck has been developing the country as a core hub in its supply chain for next-generation chip materials.
